stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
explain: Linguistics describes language at several levels: phonology (sounds), morphology (word forms), syntax (sentence structure), semantics (meaning) and pragmatics (use in context). French syntax is largely SVO with clitic pronouns before the verb: "Je le lui donne." Its tense system combines tense (when) with aspect (how the action unfolds): the imparfait is imperfective, the passé composé perfective.

Mood and modality matter: the subjunctive marks non-assertion rather than a time. Participle agreement follows a syntactic rule: with avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before the verb ("Les lettres que j'ai écrites"). The "passé simple" survives mainly in literary narrative, while the passé composé covers spoken narration.
sentences: The letters that I wrote are here.

gq.q: Choose the correct form: Les lettres que j'ai ___
gq.why: The direct object les lettres precedes the verb, so the participle agrees.

gq.q: Why is "J'ai écrit les lettres" without agreement?
o: The direct object follows the verb
gq.why: Agreement happens only with a preceding direct object.

panel.q: What does aspect describe?
o: How an action unfolds in time

panel.q: In "Je le lui donne", what do le and lui represent?
o: The direct object and the indirect object

panel.q: Why is the subjunctive better described as marking non-assertion than a time?
o: It appears in present and past forms and signals attitude
It always refers to the future

teach.model: Linguistics studies sounds (phonology), word forms (morphology), sentence structure (syntax), meaning (semantics) and use (pragmatics). French combines tense and aspect, uses clitic pronouns before the verb and applies participle agreement with a preceding direct object.

stages.hook: Why does French need both a "passé simple" and a "passé composé" for what looks like the same past, and what does linguistics say about it?
stages.mnemonic: Sounds, forms, structure, meaning, use: five lenses on one language.

trip.prompt: Find the part on tense, mood or aspect and note one example in French.

stages.title: Historical development of the language
explain: French descends from the spoken Latin of Gaul, shaped by Celtic substrates and Germanic (Frankish) superstrates. The Strasbourg Oaths of 842 are among the earliest texts in a Romance vernacular. Old French (about 9th to 13th century) had case endings and verb-second tendencies; by Middle French (14th to 16th century) cases were lost.

The Ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts (1539) made French the language of legal documents in France. The Académie française was founded in 1635 to regulate the language. Spelling preserved etymological letters even as sounds changed: "doigt" (from Latin digitus) keeps a g that has not been pronounced for centuries. The Renaissance revived Latin forms, creating doublets like "frêle" and "fragile".

gq.q: Which text is among the earliest in a Romance vernacular?
gq.why: The oaths of 842 are an early French document.

gq.q: Why does "doigt" keep a silent g?
o: Spelling preserves its Latin origin digitus
gq.why: Etymological spelling kept letters after sounds changed.

panel.q: What did the Ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts (1539) establish?
panel.why: It replaced Latin in official legal use.

panel.q: What are doublets like "frêle" and "fragile"?
o: Two words from the same Latin source, one inherited and one borrowed
panel.why: Popular and learned routes yield pairs.

panel.q: Why did spoken French change more than written French?
o: Pronunciation evolves continuously while spelling is standardised

teach.model: French developed from spoken Latin in Gaul with Celtic and Frankish influence. The Strasbourg Oaths (842) are an early text. The Ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts (1539) made French the legal language. Spelling kept etymological letters, so it differs from sound.

stages.hook: Why is French so close to Spanish and Italian but so different in spelling from its pronunciation?
stages.mnemonic: The ear moved on; the spelling stayed behind.

trip.prompt: Find the periods of French history and note which one the Strasbourg Oaths belong to.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
explain: Cultural discourse analysis reads texts in their contexts. Voltaire's "Candide" (1759) uses satire to challenge optimism. Flaubert's "Madame Bovary" (1857) is famous for its use of free indirect discourse. Simone de Beauvoir's "Le Deuxième Sexe" (1949) argued that womanhood is socially constructed. Frantz Fanon's "Peau noire, masques blancs" (1952) analysed colonial psychology.

Francophone literature is wide: Ousmane Sembène's "Les Bouts de bois de Dieu" (Senegal), Assia Djebar (Algeria), Kourouma's "Les Soleils des indépendances" (Côte d'Ivoire) which bends French to fit Malinké rhythms, Édouard Glissant (Martinique) and his idea of "créolisation", and Anne Hébert (Quebec). The canon is contested: who is read, taught and translated reflects power.
sentences: Kourouma adapts French to his language.

gq.q: Which writer from Martinique developed the idea of créolisation?
What is distinctive about Flaubert's free indirect discourse?
o: The narrator blends into a character's thoughts without quotation
It uses only the first person
gq.why: It merges narrator voice and character voice.

panel.q: Why is the literary canon described as contested?
o: Choices of what is taught reflect power and history
panel.why: Debate concerns which voices are included.

panel.q: What does Kourouma do in "Les Soleils des indépendances"?
o: He reshapes French with the rhythm of Malinké

panel.q: Why can a text be read both aesthetically and politically?
o: Form and context both carry meaning

points.ask: How do I read a text?
Which writers add to French literature?

teach.model: Read a text in its context. Voltaire used satire, Flaubert used free indirect discourse, Beauvoir argued about gender and Fanon about colonial psychology. Francophone writers like Kourouma and Glissant reshape French. The canon is a matter of debate.

stages.hook: How can the same novel be read as a story, a political statement and a cultural document?
stages.mnemonic: A text is a conversation with its time.

trip.prompt: Find the plot summary and note what Candide learns about optimism.

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
explain: Advanced academic writing in French follows the dissertation or commentaire composé. A strong paper has an argument, not just information. It makes a thesis claim, anticipates objections, and uses evidence. Paragraphs follow the pattern assertion, evidence, analysis.

Style: nominal structures, hedging ("il semble que", "on peut supposer que"), and precise connectors: "en revanche", "dès lors", "de surcroît". "Il semble que" normally takes the subjunctive, while "il me semble que" takes the indicative. Citations follow a style guide. Avoid plagiarism by quoting precisely and acknowledging sources.
items: la note de bas de page
sentences: This paper defends a clear thesis.
It seems that the data support the claim.

gq.q: What makes an academic paper different from a summary?
gq.why: A thesis claim organises the paper.

gq.q: Why do academic writers use hedging like "il semble que"?
o: To express claims with proper caution
gq.why: Hedging reflects the strength of evidence.

panel.q: Which structure is typical of a paragraph?
After "Il semble que" (without "me"), which mood is normally used?
panel.why: Il semble que (without certainty) takes the subjunctive; il me semble que takes the indicative.

panel.q: Why must sources be acknowledged precisely?
o: It respects authors and lets readers verify

teach.model: Academic writing in French defends a thesis with evidence and analysis. Use hedging, precise connectors and consider objections. Cite sources and avoid plagiarism.

stages.hook: What distinguishes a university essay from a school essay in French?

trip.prompt: Find the part on citation or structure and note how a claim should be supported.

stages.title: Professional translation
explain: Professional translation requires domain knowledge, terminology management and quality control. Legal translation must be precise: "shall" becomes "doit" or the future ("sera tenue d'indemniser"). Technical terms must be consistent across the document, using glossaries and translation memories.

Translators distinguish text types: informative, expressive and operative. Marketing needs adaptation (transcreation), while legal texts need fidelity. Quality control includes revision by a second person and checking numbers, names and dates. Ethics: confidentiality, competence and honesty about limits. Machine translation can help but needs post-editing.
sentences: The party must indemnify the buyer.

gq.q: Why is marketing text often adapted rather than translated literally?
o: Its effect on readers matters more than its words

panel.q: What is post-editing?
panel.why: It improves output from machine translation.

panel.q: What is a translation memory?
o: A database of previously translated segments

panel.q: Why must translators know their limits?
o: Mistakes in specialised texts can have serious consequences

teach.model: A translator needs domain knowledge, consistent terminology and revision. Use glossaries and translation memories. Adapt marketing text and keep legal text faithful. Machine translation needs post-editing.

stages.hook: How would a professional translator handle a contract clause such as "The party shall indemnify..."?
stages.mnemonic: Know the field, keep terms consistent, revise twice.

trip.prompt: Find the challenges of legal translation and note one reason precision matters.

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
explain: Interpreting complex communication requires pragmatic skill: understanding what is implied, not just said. In "Il fait un peu froid ici" a speaker may be asking someone to close a window. Interpreters must decide how much to make explicit and how to convey tone, irony and politeness.

Cognitive load is high in simultaneous interpreting: listening, analysing, reformulating and monitoring output almost at once. Strategies include anticipation, chunking, compression and décalage (lag) of a few seconds. In diplomacy and conferences, interpreters use notes in consecutive mode and rely on preparation of terminology.
sentences: He suggests more than he says.

gq.q: What does an interpreter need beyond vocabulary?
Why is "Il fait un peu froid ici" a challenge?
o: It may be a request, not a weather report

panel.q: What is décalage in simultaneous interpreting?
o: The short lag behind the speaker

panel.q: Why is preparation of terminology essential?
o: Specialised terms cannot be improvised under pressure

panel.q: Why might an interpreter soften or keep a harsh remark?
o: Fidelity includes tone, so choices follow ethical rules
panel.why: Professional codes require faithful rendering of tone.

teach.model: An interpreter conveys meaning, tone and implication, not only words. Simultaneous interpreting involves high cognitive load, so interpreters use anticipation, chunking and lag. They prepare terminology before the event.

stages.hook: How can an interpreter capture irony, implication and tone, not only the words?
stages.mnemonic: Hear the meaning, not just the words.

trip.prompt: Find the modes of interpreting and note which one uses booths.

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
explain: Dialectology studies how varieties differ across space and social groups, mapping features with isoglosses (lines on a map where a feature changes). In Quebec, "joual" names a working-class urban speech style once stigmatised and later celebrated in literature and theatre. In France, the langues d'oïl (including Picard and Norman) and langues d'oc (Occitan) developed alongside standard French. Regional accents vary: in the south, final e is often pronounced. Quebec French has features such as affrication of t and d before high vowels and words like "tuque" for a winter hat.

Louisiana French (Cajun and Creole) developed from Acadian and other settlers. Haitian Creole is a separate language with French-derived vocabulary and its own grammar. African Frenches show contact with Wolof, Bambara and other languages. Linguists describe variation by systematic rules and attitudes; the "standard" is a social construct with prestige, not a purely linguistic superiority.
sentences: Occitan is not a dialect of French.

gq.why: Occitan belongs to the Romance family in southern France.

gq.q: Why is "standard French" called a social construct?
o: Its prestige comes from history and institutions, not linguistic quality
It is the only written form

panel.q: What is Haitian Creole?
o: A distinct language with French-derived vocabulary
panel.why: It has its own grammar and standard.

panel.q: What do isoglosses show?
o: The geographic boundary of a linguistic feature

panel.q: Why do attitudes matter in dialectology?
o: They influence which varieties are valued or stigmatised
panel.why: Language attitudes shape standardisation and education.

teach.model: Dialectology studies how language varies by place and social group. French has regional accents, langues d'oïl and d'oc, Quebec, Louisiana and African varieties, and Creoles like Haitian. All varieties follow rules.

stages.hook: Is "joual", "cajun French" or Haitian Creole just "bad French"?
stages.mnemonic: Variation is a pattern, not a mistake.

trip.prompt: Find what an isogloss is and describe one example.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
explain: Scientific and technical French values precision, impersonality and terminology. Terms come from Greek and Latin roots ("hémoglobine", "photosynthèse") and are standardised by commissions. France's terminology commissions propose French equivalents for English terms: "ordinateur" for computer, "courriel" for email in Quebec and in some official texts, and "logiciel" for software.

Typical features: the present for general truths ("L'eau bout à 100 °C"), passive and impersonal forms ("il est observé que"), noun phrases with de ("la vitesse de la lumière"), and numerals with a comma as decimal separator: 3,14. The metric system and SI units are the norm. Abstracts follow a fixed form: contexte, méthode, résultats, conclusion.

gq.q: Which tense states general scientific truths?
gq.why: The present is the tense of general facts.

gq.q: Why is the decimal separator a comma in French science texts?
o: French uses a comma as the decimal separator
gq.why: In French, 3,14 is three point fourteen.

panel.q: What is "logiciel"?
panel.why: It was created as a French equivalent.

panel.q: Why are terms made from Greek and Latin roots?
Why do terminology commissions propose French equivalents?
o: To keep French usable in modern fields
panel.why: Language planning aims for full-domain use.

teach.model: Scientific French is precise and impersonal. It uses the present for general truths, passive and impersonal structures, Greek and Latin roots, and SI units. Decimals use a comma. Commissions create French terms like logiciel.

stages.hook: Why does scientific French use the passive and the impersonal so much, and how are new terms created?
stages.mnemonic: Precise terms, present tense, impersonal voice.

trip.prompt: Find the official status of French and note one country outside France where it is official.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
explain: The integrated project brings skills together. Choose a topic, such as language and identity in the Francophone world. Gather sources, build a thesis, plan an outline and write in the right register. Present with a clear structure and answer questions in real time.

Evaluate your own work: Is the grammar accurate (agreement, subjunctive, tenses)? Is the vocabulary precise? Are sources cited? Is the register consistent? Does the argument answer the question? Include a short translation of a key passage and justify your choices.
sentences: This project explores language and identity.
The thesis is supported by sources.

gq.q: What is the first step in a project?
o: Choose a focused topic and question
gq.why: A clear focus guides everything else.

o: It identifies strengths and errors to correct

panel.q: What would show register control?
o: Consistent forms such as vous and formal vocabulary

panel.q: Why justify translation choices?
o: It shows reasoning about meaning and context

panel.q: What makes a thesis testable?
o: It can be supported or challenged with evidence
panel.why: A thesis is a claim, not a topic.

teach.model: A project combines a clear question, a thesis, evidence, accurate language and a suitable register. Present it clearly, cite sources and reflect on your own errors. Justify translation choices.

stages.hook: Can you now plan, draft and present a complete French project that combines grammar, culture, translation and argument?

trip.prompt: Find the stages of a project and note which stage comes before the work begins.
